## Dr. Nathan Furey's Fish and Movement Ecology Lab:

### 1. Forage Fish Energy Density

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Kimberly A. Lato, Nathan B. Furey

Forage Fish are important prey for many organisms because they connect
and disperse energy across food webs. Higher availability of energy
dense forage fish is correlated with higher ecosystem productivity and
resilience to ecosystem stressors such as warming. This study collects
forage fish samples from several sources: seine surveys, dropped prey items at White
Island's tern colony, and directly from the stomach contents of striped
bass (*Morone saxatilis*) and Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*). Samples are
dried, homogenized, and pressed into pellets. These pellets are then
combusted using a bomb calorimeter to learn how much energy is contained
in one gram of sample. Prey species with a higher energy density have
higher value to predators, so changes in prey energetics can alter
predator foraging effort and food webs.

![](images/RARGOM26%20ED%20Poster%20Final%206.pdf)

### 2. Stomach Contents of Striped Bass (*Morone saxatilis*) and Atlantic Cod (*Gadus morhua*)

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Atlas Emmanuel, Sidney Axtell, Nathan B.
Furey

Atlantic cod and striped bass are economically and ecologically
important generalist predators in Gulf of Maine fisheries. The quality
of their diets may affect their capacity to adapt to warming waters.
This project collects stomach contents from these species through
gastric lavage (nonlethal; stomach flushing) to identify what these
predators are eating. Data on prey energetics from project 1 will be
coupled with data on prey species abundance from this study to gain a
better picture of diet quality.

### 3. Rainbow smelt (*Osmerus mordax*) Aging

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Matt Scott, Shae Shandroff, Trevor
Banister, Nathan B. Furey

Rainbow smelt are important prey for species such as striped bass
(*Morone saxatilis*), Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*), and Atlantic salmon
(*Salmo salar*) while also supporting New Hampshire ice fisheries. The
Furey Lab tags smelt to better understand migration and spawning
behavior, which offers an opportunity to collect morphometric data and
fish scale samples. I clean and age these scales in an effort to assign
each fish and its morphometric data to a yearly cohort. Understanding
which yearly cohorts had higher growth and survival can then allow us to
plot these data alongside environmental data and identify the
environmental factors that affect smelt population success.

## Dr. Karolina Kwasek's Aquaculture Lab

### Effects of Simulating Natural Environment on Zebrafish (*Danio rerio*) Growth and Survival

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Simon Laidlaw, Juliana Sanzi, Jessica
Robinson, Karolina Kwasek

Past aquaculture studies have shown that increasing environmental
complexity can positively impact fish growth and survival in
aquaculture. This can take many forms, from adding plants to adding
images/actual substrate. The natural habitat of Zebrafish is freshwater
floodplains characterized by silt and vegetation, so we are seeing if
images of silt and addition of vegetation improves zebrafish growth and
survival. Zebrafish are essentially the lab rats of the sea so any
improvement in culturing practices could benefit several industries
using zebrafish as a model organism.

### Replacing Rotifers (*Brachionus plicatilis*) with Decapsulated *Artemia* as a Means of Improving Current Zebrafish (*Danio rerio*) Culture Practices

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Jessica Robinson, Karolina Kwasek

Zebrafish are a vertebrate model organism used for research in many
industries, from human health to neurobiology. This study aimed to
improve larval rearing practices during which high mortality is
typically observed. Rotifers, a common larval feed for zebrafish, are
unpredictable and time intensive to culture so this study replaced them
with decapsulated *Artemia* nauplii and tested growth and survival.
Results showed zebrafish fed decapsulated *Artemia* had higher survival
and comparable growth. Thus, this study's experimental feeding regime
could become a standardized feeding protocol for raising larval
zebrafish.

Peer reviewed publication coming soon!

## Upcoming Projects

### Development of Scallop Aquaculture 

Contributors: Esher Swanson, Lyla Tulloch, Kaitlyn Ilacqua, Emily Kumph, Michael Coogan, Michael Doherty, David Fredrikkson

We will study methods of optimizing sustainable scallop farming in the Gulf of Maine using marine-mammal-safe equipment and create a potential business model.
